📚 Reference Links

  • 202 Accepted and Retry-After (normative) — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

  • 202 semantics and the Location convention — MDN: 202 Accepted

  • Error envelope for job failures — RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

  • Streaming the result instead of polling for it — WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events

  • Bonus — Amazon Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does 202 actually promise? Accepted for processing. Not started, not succeeded — only that you have a handle.
Which two headers make 202 usable? Location (the status resource) and Retry-After (how soon to poll).
Status code when the job is done? 200 on the status resource with a terminal state, or 303 See Other pointing at the result.
Why does a job need an idempotency key? Otherwise a retried submit creates a second expensive job you'll pay for twice.
The default gateway timeout you're fighting? 60s at most L7 load balancers — the reason holding the request open fails.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

When work outlasts a request, you stop holding the connection and make the job a resource. POST returns 202 Accepted with a Location pointing at a status resource and a Retry-After telling the client how soon to check. The client polls that resource until it reaches a terminal state, then follows a link to the result. The alternatives are a webhook callback, when the client has a reachable endpoint, and streaming, when there's partial output worth showing as it's produced. Holding the request open is the option that isn't available — your load balancer will cut it at sixty seconds.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why not just hold the request open for two minutes?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the specific things that break, or just have a general sense that it's bad.

Four things break, in this order. The load balancer cuts it first — 60 seconds is the common default, and the client gets a 504 while the work carries on server-side, which is the worst outcome because the caller now doesn't know whether it happened. Then intermediate proxies and CDNs with their own read timeouts. Then the client's own HTTP timeout, often 30 seconds by default in SDKs. And finally your own capacity: a held request occupies a worker or a connection, so long jobs consume concurrency you need for short requests.

The deeper problem is that the request/response model has no way to express "still working". A held connection is indistinguishable from a hung one to every intermediary between you and the client, so all of them apply their own liveness heuristics and one of them will act. Making the job a resource removes the ambiguity entirely: the submit is fast, the state is queryable, and nothing has to guess.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Polling, callback, or streaming?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up on any "design a batch/LLM/report API" round.

🎯 Really testing: whether you choose on the client's reachability and on whether partial output has value.

Polling is the default because it works for every client. No inbound connectivity required, no delivery guarantees to reason about, trivially resumable — a client can crash, restart, and check the job's state. The cost is wasted requests, which Retry-After and exponential backoff bound, and latency of up to one poll interval after completion.

Callbacks invert it: you POST the result to a URL the client supplied. That's efficient and immediate, and it drags in a whole second system — signature verification so the client can trust it's you, retries with backoff because their endpoint will be down sometimes, a DLQ, replay protection, and an SSRF review because you're now making outbound requests to a user-supplied URL. Worth it for server-to-server integrations at volume, absurd for a browser client that can't receive one anyway.

Streaming applies when there's meaningful partial output — tokens from a model, rows from an export, progress from a long transform. It gives the best perceived latency and it's the shape LLM products need. It's the wrong answer when the result is atomic (a rendered PDF, a completed payment batch) because there's nothing to stream but progress percentages, and a poll gives you those more cheaply.

The pattern most large systems land on is polling as the baseline, with a callback offered for server clients and streaming layered on top when partial results exist — and all three reading the same job resource, so they're views rather than parallel implementations.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Ten thousand clients polling a job endpoint every second. What breaks?

📍 Seen in the wild: the scaling probe once you've chosen polling.

What breaks is your API tier serving status checks rather than work. Ten thousand jobs polled every second is 10k rps of reads that mostly return "still running", and if each read hits the primary database to fetch job state, you've built a synthetic load generator pointed at your own datastore. It's self-inflicted and it scales with the number of in-flight jobs, which is exactly the number that rises during an incident when jobs are slow.

Three controls fix it, and they compose. Retry-After on every 202 and every non-terminal status response, with a value that grows — 1 second early, 5 after a minute, 30 after ten — so clients that respect it self-throttle. Job state cached in a fast store with a short TTL, so a status read never touches the primary. And a per-client rate limit on the status endpoint returning 429 with Retry-After, because some clients will ignore your hint and a hint is not a control.

It presents as database load correlated with job duration rather than job volume: jobs get slower, so more are in flight, so polling rises, so the database gets slower. That feedback loop is the reason to instrument polls-per-job as a metric — a rising value means clients are ignoring Retry-After and you're one incident away from amplifying your own slowdown.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the job API for expensive LLM batch work — minutes to hours, costly to re-run.

🎯 Really testing: whether you protect against duplicate expensive work and design for resumption rather than completion.

The highest-stakes constraint is cost: a re-run isn't just latency, it's GPU-minutes billed twice. So the submit endpoint requires an idempotency key and the key maps to the job id, which means a client retrying a lost 202 gets the same job back rather than starting a second one. That single decision is worth more than anything else in the design.

The job is a resource with an explicit state machine — queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled — and a monotonically increasing progress field, so a client can tell "slow" from "stuck". Results live at a separate URL with their own retention policy, because a job record is small and cheap to keep for months while a multi-gigabyte output is not; the status response links to it rather than embedding it. Cancellation is a real endpoint, because on expensive work the ability to stop is a cost control, and it must be honoured by the worker, not just recorded.

The delivery layer is polling by default, with SSE available on the job resource for clients that want tokens as they're produced, and an optional signed callback for server-to-server clients. All three read the same state; none is a separate code path.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is jobs in a non-terminal state past their expected duration — the stuck-job class. It's the one that never errors, keeps a client polling forever, and consumes capacity while producing nothing, so it needs an explicit reaper with a timeout per job type.

4. Quick Comparison Table

202 + polling Callback / webhook Streaming (SSE) Hold the request open
Client must be reachable no yes, publicly no no
Latency to notice completion up to one poll interval immediate immediate + partial output immediate
Cost profile wasted reads, bounded by Retry-After one delivery per job one connection per job one connection per job
Resumable after client crash trivially needs your retry policy yes, with a sequence id no — the result is lost
You must build a status resource signing, retries, DLQ, SSRF review buffering exemptions, resume nothing, and it won't work
When you'd actually pick it the default, all clients server-to-server at volume partial output has value (tokens, rows) never past ~30s

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Take the ticket, don't wait at the counter.

📖 Story

You hand in a repair and the clerk gives you a numbered ticket and says "check back in about an hour." You don't stand there — the shop would run out of standing room, and the security guard would move you on long before the repair was done anyway. When you come back, the ticket tells you the state; when it's ready, it tells you which shelf to collect from. Hand in the same job twice with the same ticket number and you get the same repair back, not two bills.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • the numbered ticket = 202 Accepted plus Location, the handle to a job resource

  • "check back in about an hour" = Retry-After, the server's control over poll rate

  • the shop running out of standing room = held requests consuming worker concurrency

  • the security guard moving you on = the load balancer's 60-second idle timeout cutting a held request

  • same ticket, one bill = the idempotency key mapping a retried submit onto the existing job

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The job state machine

The contract is the state machine, not the endpoints. queued → running → {succeeded, failed, cancelled}, with running optionally carrying monotonic progress. Two rules make it usable: terminal states are terminal — a client that sees succeeded never needs to poll again — and every non-terminal response carries Retry-After, so the server controls poll rate rather than the client guessing. failed carries a problem document per RFC 9457 with a stable type, so clients can distinguish "retry this" from "your input was wrong".

The polling math

A client polling at interval T for a job of duration D makes D/T requests and learns of completion up to T late. Fleet-wide, with J concurrent jobs, the status endpoint sees J/T rps — and J rises when jobs slow down, which is precisely when you can least afford it. Constant-interval polling is therefore the wrong default; a growing interval (1s, then 2, 5, 15, 30, capped) makes the request count O(log D) instead of O(D), and the extra completion latency is proportional to how long the job already ran, which is exactly the right shape — nobody minds hearing about a two-hour job thirty seconds late.

The other number worth carrying is the duplicate-work cost: without an idempotency key, a client's retry after a lost 202 starts a second job. At LLM batch scale that is a doubled bill with no error anywhere, which is why the key is a cost control rather than a correctness nicety.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is 504s and duplicate work, and both come from the same root: pretending slow work fits the request/response model. A held request produces gateway timeouts where the client cannot tell whether the work happened, and the client's natural response — retry — is what creates the duplicate. Making the job a resource removes both at once, because the submit is fast and the retry is idempotent.

The second observable is status-endpoint load, which is entirely self-inflicted and entirely controllable. Retry-After plus a cached state read turns polling from a scaling risk into a rounding error, and skipping both is how a job API becomes the biggest source of database reads in the system — proportional to in-flight jobs, and therefore worst exactly during an incident.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

POST /v1/batch-jobs HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: 5f2c-a1                 # a retried submit returns the SAME job, not a second one
Content-Type: application/json

{"input_url":"s3://bucket/prompts.jsonl","model":"m-large"}

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Location: /v1/batch-jobs/j_91b           # the status resource — the whole contract hangs off this
Retry-After: 2                            # server-controlled poll rate, not the client's guess
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"j_91b","state":"queued","created_at":"2026-09-04T09:12:00Z"}

GET /v1/batch-jobs/j_91b HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Retry-After: 30                           # grows as the job ages — O(log D) polls, not O(D)
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"j_91b","state":"running","progress":0.42,
 "expires_at":"2026-09-11T09:12:00Z"}     # result retention, published so clients don't assume forever

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Scenario: the batch API above. A 22-minute job; the client's first 202 response is lost.

📥 [1] 09:12:00 POST /v1/batch-jobs  Idempotency-Key: 5f2c-a1
    │      job j_91b upserted (key → id), enqueued, 202 written…
    ▼
❌ [2] …response lost in transit. Client has no job id and no idea if it exists.
    │
    ▼
🔄 [3] 09:12:03 client retries the identical POST with the SAME key
    │      server finds the key → returns 202 with Location /v1/batch-jobs/j_91b
    │      ONE job. Without the key: two 22-minute GPU jobs, one bill each.
    ▼
⏱️ [4] polls at 2s, 5s, 15s, 30s, 60s… (following Retry-After) → 28 polls over 22 min
    │      constant 2s polling would have been 660 polls for the same information
    ▼
🤖 [5] 09:34:10 worker finishes; state=succeeded, result_url set, expires_at +7d
    │
    ▼
🎯 [6] 09:34:38 next poll returns succeeded (28s after completion — nobody minds on a 22-min job)
    │
    ▼
📦 [7] GET /v1/batch-jobs/j_91b/result → 200, 340 MB, streamed from object storage

1. Steps 1–3 are the entire argument for idempotency keys on job submission. A lost response is indistinguishable from a failed request, so the client must retry, and without the key that retry is a second expensive job. The key turns "did it work?" from an unanswerable question into a lookup.

2. The Retry-After progression in step 4 saved 632 requests for one job. Multiply by concurrent jobs to see why it matters: at 10,000 in-flight jobs, constant 2-second polling is 5,000 rps of status reads; the growing schedule is roughly two orders of magnitude less. It costs one header.

3. Step 6's 28-second detection lag is a deliberate trade, and the right one. Completion latency proportional to elapsed job time means short jobs are noticed quickly and long jobs tolerate a longer gap — which matches how users actually perceive it. A fixed interval optimises for the wrong end.

4. Step 7 separates the result from the job record on purpose. The job document is a few hundred bytes and worth keeping for months for audit; the 340 MB output is not. Publishing expires_at makes retention an explicit contract rather than something a client discovers by getting a 410 one day.

5. What isn't in this trace is a held connection, and that's the point. No hop between client and API ever saw a request that lasted longer than a few milliseconds, so no load balancer, proxy or client SDK timeout had an opinion. That's what makes the pattern work through infrastructure you don't control.

10. When TO Use This

  • Any operation that can exceed ~10 seconds — well before the 60-second timeout, because the margin is what protects you when the work is slower than usual.

  • Expensive or non-repeatable work — LLM batch inference, video transcode, large exports, report generation. The job resource is what makes retries safe and cancellation possible.

  • Work whose duration varies by orders of magnitude — a job resource serves a 200 ms case and a 6-hour case with one interface, where a synchronous endpoint has to be designed for the worst case.

  • When the client is a browser — it can't receive a callback, so 202 plus polling (or SSE on the job) is the only shape available.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not for work that finishes in under a second. The ceremony — a job record, a status endpoint, a second round trip — costs the client more than the wait. Return the answer.

  • Not with callbacks to arbitrary user-supplied URLs without an SSRF review. You're making outbound requests to a destination the caller chose, which is a server-side request forgery primitive unless you validate the target and egress through a controlled path.

  • Not with an unbounded result retention. "The result URL works forever" becomes a storage bill and a compliance problem. Publish expires_at from the first release; adding expiry later breaks clients.

  • Not without a stuck-job reaper. A job that never reaches a terminal state polls forever and holds capacity. Every job type needs a maximum duration and something that transitions it to failed when exceeded.

  • Not as a way to hide a synchronous dependency's slowness from yourself. If a job is slow because a downstream service is degraded, the queue makes it invisible rather than better — you've moved the symptom, and the backlog arithmetic still applies.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "202 Accepted means the work started."

✅ Reality: It means the request was accepted for processing — possibly queued, possibly rejected later by a validator, possibly never run at all. It's an acknowledgement of intent, and that's exactly why it must come with a Location you can query, or the client has been told nothing useful.

❌ Misconception: "Webhooks are the modern replacement for polling."

✅ Reality: They're an optimisation available only to clients with a reachable, authenticated endpoint, and they bring signing, retries, DLQs, replay protection and an SSRF review with them. Nearly every serious job API offers callbacks and keeps polling, because polling is the one that always works.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated Retry-After as advisory decoration. It's the only lever the server has over aggregate poll load, and a growing value turns polling cost from linear in job duration to logarithmic. Combined with a 429 for clients that ignore it, it's the difference between polling being free and polling being the top query in your database.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Proposing "just increase the load-balancer timeout". It moves the failure rather than fixing it — the client SDK, the CDN, or the next proxy still has an opinion, and you've made every held request consume a worker for minutes. Naming the timeout as a symptom rather than the problem is the senior framing.

Designing the happy path and skipping cancellation. On expensive work, cancellation is a cost control, and it has to be honoured by the worker rather than merely recorded in the job row. Its absence is the first thing someone will ask about.

Forgetting the idempotency key on submit. Every other part of the design can be right and a lost 202 still doubles the bill. This is the highest-value single line in the whole pattern.

Treating polling load as the client's problem. It's yours: you control it with Retry-After, caching and rate limits. An answer that shrugs at 10k rps of status checks hasn't run one of these.

No answer for stuck jobs. Non-terminal forever is the failure mode that produces no errors, no alerts and infinite polling. If your state machine has no timeout, it isn't finished.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
202 Accepted "accepted, not completed" Pair with Location for the status resource RFC 9110 §15.3.3
Retry-After seconds or HTTP-date Valid on 202, 429 and 503; the server's poll-rate control RFC 9110 §10.2.3
303 See Other redirect to the result The idiomatic "done, fetch it here" response RFC 9110 §15.4.4
Common L7 LB idle timeout 60s Why holding the request open fails AWS ELB / nginx docs
nginx proxy_read_timeout 60s default The second hop that cuts a held request nginx docs
Polling cost, fixed interval D/T requests per job 22-min job at 2s ⇒ 660 requests Arithmetic
Polling cost, growing interval O(log D) Same job ⇒ ~28 requests Arithmetic
Failure envelope application/problem+json Terminal failed state carries a stable type RFC 9457

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Polling adds up to one interval of completion lag; streaming removes it and costs a connection per job
💰 Cost Idempotency keys prevent duplicate expensive work; result retention is a storage bill you must bound explicitly
🔒 Security / visibility Callbacks make you an outbound HTTP client to user-supplied URLs — SSRF, signing and egress control all become yours
📈 Scale Status load scales with in-flight jobs, which rises exactly when jobs are slow; Retry-After plus caching is the control
🔧 Ops complexity A job store, a queue, a worker fleet, a reaper and a retention policy — meaningfully more machinery than a synchronous endpoint
🐛 Debuggability Excellent, if the job id appears in the submit response, every log line and every trace; poor if the job is anonymous work in a queue

16. Real World Usage

LLM batch APIs are the current canonical example: submit a file of prompts, get a job id, poll for state, download results, with an explicit expiry on the output — and the idempotency-key requirement is there precisely because a duplicated batch is a duplicated GPU bill.

Cloud provider control planes model provisioning as long-running operations with their own resource type and their own polling contract, which is why creating infrastructure returns an operation id rather than the created resource.

Media processing and export pipelines combine all three delivery styles in the way the framework predicts: polling for the browser, signed callbacks for server-to-server customers, and progress streaming where partial output exists — three views of one job resource.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 97-sync-vs-async.md — the fork this pattern implements over HTTP

  • 67-idempotency-keys.md — the mechanism that makes a retried submit safe

  • 60-choosing-the-right-code.md — 202 vs 200 vs 303, and 429 with Retry-After

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 95-webhooks.md — the callback half, in full

  • 71-server-sent-events.md — the streaming half, in full

  • 96-queues-and-event-streams.md — what runs the work behind the job resource

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Streaming the whole operation (SSE/WebSocket) — when partial output is the product, as in token streaming

  • A queue with no HTTP surface — when the submitter is internal and doesn't need a status resource

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Object storage with presigned URLs — how large results leave the API tier without passing through it

  • A reaper / watchdog — the component that gives non-terminal jobs a terminal state

  • Cross-folder: batch inference and continuous batching → LLM folder (serving); backlog behaviour → 96-queues-and-event-streams.md

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

"Design an API for generating large reports / running batch inference / transcoding video" is the framing, and the whole answer is this pattern. The probe is whether you reach for a job resource immediately rather than negotiating timeouts, whether you protect against duplicate expensive work, and whether you have an answer for polling load and for jobs that never finish. It's also the standard follow-up to any LLM-serving design once the word "batch" appears.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
1k in-flight jobs Status reads hit the primary database Cache job state with a short TTL; Retry-After growth schedule
100k in-flight jobs Status endpoint dominates API traffic; queue depth and worker cost Per-client status rate limits with 429; autoscale workers on oldest-message age
10M jobs/day Result storage and retention bill; job-record volume Presigned URLs straight to object storage, tiered retention, archive job records out of the hot store

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, polling becomes the largest read workload in the system, and it grows precisely when jobs slow down.

  • At 100x, result storage retention — not compute — is the dominant cost line, and nobody set an expiry in the first release.

  • Operationally, the 3am version is a worker fleet that crashed mid-job: dozens of jobs stuck in running forever, clients polling indefinitely, and no reaper to move them to failed.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Job duration p50/p99 by job type, with an explicit expected-duration SLO — this is what the reaper's timeout is derived from.

  • Count of non-terminal jobs older than their expected duration — the stuck-job detector; should normally be zero.

  • Polls per job — a rising value means clients are ignoring Retry-After, and it precedes a database load incident.

  • Idempotency-key hit rate on submit — a nonzero rate is healthy (retries are being deduped); a spike means clients are failing to receive responses.

Why did the AI ecosystem standardise on HTTP + SSE rather than WebSocket or gRPC?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
MCP over stdio or over Streamable HTTP?
What actually goes wrong, and it's never the protocol

notes.html:
🧭 Index amendment. The index line for this item lists MCP's transports as "stdio / HTTP+SSE / streamable HTTP". As of the current specification revision, MCP defines two standard bindings — stdio and Streamable HTTP. The separate HTTP+SSE transport belongs to earlier revisions and survives only as a backward-compatibility path. Amend the index line when convenient.

📚 Reference Links

  • MCP transports (current revision) — Model Context Protocol: Transports

  • The provider streaming shape everything else copied — Claude Docs: Streaming messages

  • Agent-to-agent delegation — Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification

  • The SSE wire format all of these lean on — WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What transport does a local MCP server use? stdio — newline-delimited JSON-RPC over the standard streams of a subprocess the client launched.
What does MCP's Streamable HTTP binding do? Each message is a POST to one endpoint; the reply is a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream.
What do all three protocols here assume underneath? JSON over HTTP with SSE for anything progressive — no new wire format was invented.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The AI stack didn't invent a transport. Provider inference APIs are ordinary HTTP POST with stream: true, and the stream is SSE — one data: record per token or delta, terminating in a sentinel event. MCP, which connects a model host to tools and data, is JSON-RPC over two bindings: stdio for a locally-launched subprocess, and Streamable HTTP for a remote server, where a POST's reply may be a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream. A2A, for agent-to-agent delegation, is the same shape again — JSON-RPC over HTTP with SSE for progress. Everything you know about SSE, timeouts and buffering applies unchanged.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why did the AI ecosystem standardise on HTTP + SSE rather than WebSocket or gRPC?

Because the traffic shape is one-directional and the deployment constraints are ordinary. A completion is a single request followed by a stream of server-produced text, with no continuous upstream channel — which is exactly SSE's shape and exactly not WebSocket's. Choosing SSE meant every existing piece of infrastructure kept working: bearer-token auth, corporate proxies, API gateways, rate limiters, WAFs, access logs, retries, and curl for debugging. A WebSocket would have needed exemptions in all of those, and gRPC would have been unreachable from a browser.

The exception proves the rule: realtime voice APIs use WebSocket, because there the client is a continuous producer — audio flows upward while audio or tokens flow down, and interruption couples the directions. That's the one place in the stack where the traffic shape genuinely demands full duplex, and it's chosen deliberately rather than by default.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

MCP over stdio or over Streamable HTTP?

stdio is the local answer: the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over its standard streams. Authentication is process ownership, latency is a pipe, and there is no network surface at all — no port, no TLS, no auth server. That makes it the right binding for tools that touch the user's own machine: a filesystem, a local database, a git checkout. Its limits follow from the same properties: one client per process, lifecycle tied to the parent, and no way to reach it from anywhere else.

Streamable HTTP is the remote answer: one endpoint, each message a POST, and a reply that is either a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream when the server has progressive output. That gives you everything HTTP gives you — TLS, bearer tokens or OAuth, gateways, rate limits, horizontal scaling, standard observability — and it brings the whole SSE operational checklist with it: proxy buffering must be disabled on the streaming path, idle timeouts must exceed the longest quiet gap, and a dropped connection needs a resumption story.

The choice is really about where the capability lives. Local machine access, or a tool a single user runs, is stdio. A shared service several users or agents call is Streamable HTTP, and at that point it's an ordinary internet-facing service that needs authentication, tenancy and rate limiting designed rather than assumed.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Provider inference API MCP (stdio) MCP (Streamable HTTP) A2A
Purpose call a model host → local tool/data host → remote tool/data agent → agent delegation
Message format JSON request/response JSON-RPC JSON-RPC JSON-RPC
Transport HTTPS, SSE when streaming subprocess stdio HTTPS POST, SSE per request HTTPS, SSE for progress
Auth bearer token / API key process ownership OAuth / bearer, gateway-enforced HTTP auth on the endpoint
Streaming SSE token deltas line-delimited messages request-scoped SSE stream SSE task updates
Network surface public API none full internet-facing service full internet-facing service
When you'd actually pick it any model call local machine capabilities shared, multi-user capabilities delegating work between agent systems

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

What actually goes wrong, and it's never the protocol

Three failure classes account for nearly everything in this layer, and all three are inherited from HTTP rather than invented by these specs.

Buffering. A proxy or CDN that buffers the SSE response converts token-by-token streaming into a single delivery at the end. Time-to-first-token collapses while total latency, status code and byte count stay identical — so nothing in a standard dashboard shows it. This is the number one deployment bug for every protocol in this table.

Idle timeouts. A model that thinks for ninety seconds before emitting a token, or a tool call that takes minutes, hits a 60-second load-balancer or proxy_read_timeout default. The connection dies mid-operation. Heartbeat comments or an early keep-alive event, plus raised timeouts on the streaming path, are the fix.

Cancellation. When a client disconnects, the server often doesn't learn for seconds or minutes — a dropped TCP flow through NAT produces no FIN — so generation continues and GPU time is spent for nobody. Cancellation is best-effort by construction; MCP defines it explicitly per binding (a notification on stdio, closing the response stream on Streamable HTTP), and budgets should assume it sometimes fails to arrive.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't expose a remote MCP server without treating it as a public service. It has an endpoint, tenancy, authentication, rate limits and abuse potential like any other API. "It's just a tool server" is how an internal capability ends up reachable from the internet.

  • Don't let a model host reach arbitrary URLs on request. A tool that fetches a caller-supplied URL is an SSRF primitive with an LLM choosing the target. Egress allow-listing belongs here, not in a later hardening pass.

  • Don't assume the stream is the durable record. A dropped SSE connection loses whatever wasn't received. If the output matters, it belongs in a job resource with a buffer, not only in the connection.

  • Don't design a voice path around SSE. Audio flows upward continuously, which is the one shape SSE cannot serve. That's the WebSocket case, and it's the exception worth naming precisely.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "MCP has three transports: stdio, HTTP+SSE, and Streamable HTTP."

✅ Reality: The current specification defines two standard bindings — stdio and Streamable HTTP. HTTP+SSE was a separate transport in earlier revisions and now exists only for backward compatibility. Streamable HTTP still uses SSE, as the response form for a request that streams, which is where the confusion comes from.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I expected the agent ecosystem to need new network primitives. It needed none — every one of these protocols is JSON-RPC or JSON over HTTP with SSE for progressive output. Which means the hard problems in this layer are the familiar ones: buffering hops, idle timeouts, auth at the edge, and cancellation that doesn't arrive.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 71-server-sent-events.md — the transport all of these depend on, including its deployment traps

  • 98-long-running-jobs.md — the 202 pattern for anything slower than a stream will survive

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 102-api-authentication.md — bearer tokens and OAuth on a remote MCP endpoint

  • Cross-folder: tool use, sandboxing and agent egress security → Agentic folder; model serving and batching → LLM folder

notes.html:
📋 Table/playbook topic. Section 4 is the centrepiece and sits above Section 3. Section 5 is omitted, Section 6 is discharged by the decision flowchart, and Section 9 is a set of worked decisions rather than a packet trace.

📚 Reference Links

  • HTTP semantics, the baseline everything else is compared against — RFC 9110

  • gRPC's call types and deadlines — grpc.io: Core concepts, architecture and lifecycle

  • GraphQL's caching problem, stated by the spec's own docs — graphql.org: Caching

  • SSE semantics — WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events

  • Why a queue fails differently from a call — Amazon Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

🚀 REVISION BLOCK

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The first question, before any protocol name? Does the caller need the result to continue? Sync vs async comes before everything.
Which options a browser cannot reach directly? gRPC (needs gRPC-Web + proxy) and most brokers. Everything else is native.
Which single option gives you HTTP caching? REST. GraphQL and gRPC both give it up, and that's the underrated cost.
What makes gRPC the answer, in one word? The schema. Not speed — codegen and enforced contracts across teams.
The tiebreak when two options both work? Take the one with the lowest operational weight that still meets the requirement.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — re-read Section 4 alone.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Six options, one decision, made in four questions. First: does the caller need the result to continue — if not, it's a queue or an event, and no API protocol argument is needed. Second: is the consumer a browser, a partner, or an internal service — that eliminates gRPC for two of the three. Third: is the data flowing continuously, and in which direction — that's where SSE and WebSocket enter. Fourth: does a shared schema across teams matter enough to pay for a codegen pipeline. Everything else is preference.

4. Quick Comparison Table — the centrepiece

The full matrix

REST/JSON gRPC GraphQL SSE WebSocket Queue / event stream
Interaction request/response request/response + 4 streaming shapes request/response (query) server push full duplex fire and forget
Caller waits for result yes yes yes streams it streams it no
Consumer type anyone internal services any client, esp. many-client apps browser or any HTTP client browser or app internal / integrations
Browser reachable ✅ native ❌ needs gRPC-Web + proxy ✅ native ✅ native ✅ native ❌ not directly
Schema & codegen OpenAPI (advisory) .proto (compile-time) schema (introspectable) none none schema registry (optional)
Payload JSON protobuf (binary) JSON UTF-8 text text or binary anything
HTTP caching ✅ natively ❌ ❌ (POST) or partial n/a (stream) ❌ n/a
Latency profile one round trip per resource one, multiplexed one round trip for a whole screen continuous continuous decoupled — latency becomes staleness
Failure mode error to the caller error + DEADLINE_EXCEEDED partial data + errors array dropped connection dropped connection backlog and lag
Backpressure rejection (429/503) h2 flow control rejection h2 flow control none above TCP consumer pull rate
Ops weight low medium (h2 path, codegen, L7 LB) medium-high (query cost control) low high (connections, resume, deploys) medium-high (DLQ, lag, replay)
Debuggability curl grpcurl GraphQL tooling curl -N protocol-aware client broker tooling
When you'd actually pick it public/partner APIs, CRUD, cacheable reads internal multi-language service calls many clients needing different shapes of one graph one-way text push (tokens, feeds, progress) client streams continuously work that must happen but not now

The decision, as a flowchart

The four questions, in order

  1. Synchronous or not? Does the caller need the result to continue? If not, stop — it's a queue or an event, and the rest of the matrix doesn't apply. This is the biggest fork and it's the one people skip past.

  2. Continuous or discrete? One answer, or a stream of them? And if a stream, in which direction? One-way is SSE; two-way is WebSocket.

  3. Who is the consumer? A browser, a third party, or an internal service. This eliminates gRPC for the first two and usually eliminates GraphQL for the third.

  4. Does a shared schema justify a pipeline? Multiple languages and teams make codegen pay; one team owning both ends does not.

Tiebreak: when two options both work, take the one with the lowest operational weight. Ranked lightest to heaviest for the same job: REST < SSE < GraphQL ≈ gRPC < queue < WebSocket. That ordering is the framework's real content, because capability rarely decides and operations always do.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why does the sync/async question come before the protocol question?

🎯 Really testing: whether you see the decision as layered, or as a flat menu of six technologies.

Because it decides the failure mode, and the failure mode is what you'll live with. A synchronous choice couples you to the callee's availability, latency and — through held workers — your own capacity, so their bad ten minutes becomes your error rate and possibly a cascade. An asynchronous choice converts that into a backlog: nothing errors, everything is late, and the failure is quiet enough to run for hours unnoticed.

None of the six protocols changes that. gRPC with a deadline is still synchronous coupling; a queue with an HTTP submit endpoint is still asynchronous. Choosing REST versus gRPC after you've established the interaction is a comparatively small decision — it changes your codegen story and your caching story, not your outage story. Asking it first is how people end up defending a protocol choice that was never the question.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

GraphQL solves the round-trip problem. Why isn't it the default for public APIs?

📍 Seen in the wild: the counter-question after you've cited REST's chattiness as its weakness.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can price the costs GraphQL moves rather than removes.

It genuinely solves the round-trip problem: one request returns exactly the fields a screen needs, which is a real win for mobile clients on high-latency links and for organisations where one backend serves several very different frontends. The introspectable schema is also a better contract than most OpenAPI documents in practice, because it can't drift from the implementation.

What it costs is caching and cost control. Queries go over POST with a body that varies per client, so HTTP caching and CDN offload — REST's single biggest structural advantage — are gone, and you rebuild caching at the field level inside your own service. And because the client composes the query, the client also composes the cost: a deeply nested query can fan out into thousands of resolver calls, which is why persisted queries, depth limits, and query cost analysis are requirements rather than hardening.

For a public API that means you've handed untrusted callers a query planner. That's defensible with persisted queries — where clients can only run pre-registered documents — but at that point you've reintroduced a fixed set of endpoints with extra machinery. So GraphQL earns its place where the client diversity is real and internal; for a broad public API, REST plus a few compound endpoints is usually the cheaper answer.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The organisation has all six in production. What actually goes wrong?

📍 Seen in the wild: the "we have a mess, how do you think about it" question.

What goes wrong is not the protocols — it's that each one carries its own version of the same cross-cutting concerns, and they diverge. Authentication is a bearer token here, mTLS there, an HMAC signature on webhooks, and a token-in-first-frame on WebSocket. Retries are in the client library for gRPC, in a gateway for REST, in the broker for queues, and absent for WebSocket. Rate limiting works at the gateway for HTTP and nowhere for the other three. Tracing propagates via traceparent on HTTP, gRPC metadata, and a message header on the bus — unless someone forgot, and then a trace stops at the queue.

The consequence is that no one can answer "what happened to this request" end to end, and every incident is a manual correlation exercise. The scaling limit here is organisational: the number of distinct operational models a team can actually keep correct is small, and it's usually two.

So the answer is a deliberate policy — a default protocol per consumer type, exceptions requiring justification, and one shared story each for auth, tracing, retries and rate limiting that every protocol must implement. That's an architecture decision record, not a protocol preference, and saying so is the point of the question.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Set the API strategy for a platform with a web app, mobile apps, partner integrations and forty internal services.

🎯 Really testing: whether you'll define policy by consumer type rather than pick one winner.

The highest-stakes constraint is that these four consumer classes have genuinely different requirements, so a single protocol is a compromise imposed on all of them. The policy I'd defend: REST plus OpenAPI at the public edge for partners, because it's the only thing every integrator's language, proxy and tooling already speaks. gRPC internally, because forty services across several languages is exactly where enforced contracts and propagated deadlines pay for their pipeline. SSE for anything streaming to a browser, WebSocket only where the client streams upward. Events on a bus for anything where the caller doesn't need the result.

The composition is what keeps it from being four disconnected worlds. One gateway terminates public traffic and translates to gRPC inward, so the edge is where protocol translation lives and internal services only speak one thing. One schema repository holds both the .proto files and the OpenAPI documents, with breaking-change checks in CI. One tracing context propagated across every hop including the bus. One identity model, with tokens at the edge and mTLS inside.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is the seam: requests that cross a protocol boundary and lose their trace context. It's the failure that makes every subsequent incident twice as long, and it's invisible until you go looking — so the check is a synthetic request that traverses edge, service mesh and bus, asserting the trace is unbroken.

📖 DEPTH BLOCK

6. Mechanism & Math

Conditional section, satisfied by the decision flowchart in Section 4 — this topic is a selection framework, and each option's mechanism is covered in its own note (89, 92, 94, 71, 72, 96).

Two numbers are worth carrying into the discussion, because they're the ones people assert rather than compute.

Round trips per screen. A resource-per-entity REST design costs 1 + n requests for a parent and n children, or 2 if children can be fetched as a filtered collection. At a 120 ms mobile RTT, ten sequential children is 1.3 seconds of pure network; parallelised it's ~240 ms; in GraphQL it's one round trip. That gap — roughly 1.1 seconds — is the entire commercial argument for GraphQL, and it shrinks to nothing when the client can parallelise or when a compound endpoint exists.

Availability composition. A synchronous chain of n services each at availability a gives a^n; five hops at 99.9% is 99.5%. Every synchronous edge you add to the critical path costs availability that no single team is responsible for, which is the arithmetic behind "move it off the critical path" and the reason question one comes first.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable this decision moves is how many operational models your organisation has to keep correct. Each protocol brings its own auth story, retry semantics, rate-limiting surface, tracing propagation and debugging tooling. Two are manageable; five means every incident starts with figuring out which world you're in, and cross-cutting concerns silently diverge until a security review finds the gap.

The second is what you can change later. A REST contract with OpenAPI can be evolved additively for years. A .proto with a compatibility gate can too. A GraphQL schema is introspectable, so you can see who uses what — which is genuinely better than either. A WebSocket protocol you invented has none of that, and a queue's message format is a contract with consumers you may not know about. Choosing on capability alone ignores that the real cost is paid in year three.

9. Worked Decisions (the trace, for a table topic)

Scenario 1 — "Our mobile app needs a home screen with user, orders, and recommendations." Q1 sync (user is waiting). Q2 discrete. Q3 browser/mobile. Q4 several clients wanting different field sets? If yes → GraphQL; if the mobile team is the only consumer → REST with one compound endpoint. Defence: the round trips are the constraint, and a compound endpoint solves them without handing out a query planner.

Scenario 2 — "Checkout must reserve inventory before confirming." Q1: the caller needs the result — the confirmation is a lie without it. → Synchronous, and internal, so gRPC with a tight deadline. Defence: it's on the critical path by necessity, so bound it with a deadline and have a degraded path when inventory is down.

Scenario 3 — "Send the confirmation email after checkout." Q1: no, the caller doesn't need it. → Event on a bus, with idempotent consumers and a DLQ. Defence: email availability must never affect checkout availability, and a fourth consumer of OrderPlaced should not require changing the order service.

Scenario 4 — "Stream the assistant's answer into the chat UI." Q1 sync. Q2 continuous. Q3 client doesn't stream upward — one prompt per turn. → SSE. Defence: plain HTTP keeps the existing auth and edge, Last-Event-ID gives resume, and WebSocket's operational weight buys nothing here.

Scenario 5 — "A partner wants to know when an order ships." Q1: they're not waiting on a call — and they're a system we don't operate. → Webhook with HMAC signing, retries and a DLQ, with a polling endpoint as fallback. Defence: holding a connection to a partner's infrastructure makes their downtime our problem; push with retries plus a pull fallback is the durable shape.

Scenario 6 — "Our data team wants every order for their warehouse." Q1 no. Many consumers, historical replay needed. → Event stream with retained log, not a queue. Defence: a queue delivers each message once to one consumer; a retained log lets a new consumer start from the beginning next year without the producer knowing.

10. When TO Use This Framework

  • At the start of any design round involving service-to-service or client-to-server communication — the four questions take under a minute and stop the discussion anchoring on a technology.

  • When writing an architecture decision record — the framework's output is exactly the shape an ADR wants: the constraint, the options, the choice, the rejected alternatives.

  • When an organisation has accumulated protocols — it's the tool for defining a policy per consumer type rather than relitigating each service.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not as a substitute for measuring. The framework picks the shape. Message rate, payload size, client network conditions and query cost decide the details, and those need numbers.

  • Not to justify migrating a working system. The cost of a protocol migration is almost always larger than the benefit modelled on paper, and "it doesn't match our policy" is not by itself a reason to rewrite an integration that works.

  • Not when the real constraint is elsewhere. If your edge can't do HTTP/2 end to end, gRPC is off the table regardless of what the matrix says. Find the environmental constraints before running the questions.

  • Not for choosing a database, a broker, or a mesh. This framework is about interaction shape. It says "event stream", not "Kafka", and conflating the two skips a separate evaluation.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Pick the protocol by performance."

✅ Reality: For almost every service, database and downstream time dominate protocol overhead. What actually differs is contract enforcement, cacheability, browser reachability, failure mode and operational weight. Performance decides only at very high message rates, and then you should have the numbers.

❌ Misconception: "GraphQL replaces REST."

✅ Reality: It replaces REST's round-trip problem and gives up REST's caching, plus it hands clients control over query cost. It's a strong internal choice for many-client products and a demanding public one. Both coexist in most large platforms, deliberately.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated this as one decision. It's four, and they're ordered — sync/async first, then continuous/discrete, then consumer type, then schema. Collapsing them into "which protocol" is why these discussions go in circles: two people can be arguing about question four while disagreeing about question one.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Leading with a technology name. "We'd use Kafka" or "gRPC, obviously" answers question four before question one has been asked. State the interaction shape first; the technology falls out and the reasoning is what's being assessed.

Forgetting the browser constraint. gRPC is not directly reachable from a browser and brokers aren't either. It's a hard elimination that invalidates otherwise clean designs, and stating it early is a fast credibility win.

Ignoring what you give up. Choosing GraphQL or gRPC gives up HTTP caching. Choosing a queue gives up an immediate answer. Choosing WebSocket gives up your L7 controls. Naming the loss with the choice is what makes it a decision rather than a preference.

Treating "we'll use everything" as sophistication. Every additional protocol multiplies the cross-cutting work — auth, tracing, retries, rate limiting — and organisations reliably keep about two of them correct. A stated default per consumer type is the senior answer.

Confusing a queue with an event stream. One consumer competing for work versus many consumers of a retained fact are different designs with different replay stories. Scenario 6 exists precisely because people reach for a queue when they needed a log.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Sync chain availability a^n Five hops at 99.9% ⇒ 99.5% Composition arithmetic
Round trips, REST parent + n children 1 + n sequential, 2 parallel, 1 in GraphQL At 120 ms RTT, n = 10 ⇒ 1.3 s vs 240 ms vs 120 ms Arithmetic
gRPC call types 4 Unary, server-stream, client-stream, bidi grpc.io
GraphQL cacheability no HTTP caching over POST Field-level caching and persisted queries are the replacement graphql.org: Caching
SSE payload UTF-8 text only Binary needs base64, +33% WHATWG HTML §9.2
WebSocket frame header 2–14 bytes Per message; matters at very high message rates only RFC 6455 §5.2
Delivery semantics on a bus at-least-once Duplicates are certain; consumers must be idempotent Broker documentation

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Streaming and GraphQL reduce perceived and per-screen latency; queues remove latency from the caller and convert it into staleness
💰 Cost REST's cacheable reads are the only option in this table that can move traffic off your origin entirely
🔒 Security / visibility HTTP-shaped options keep your WAF, gateway and access logs; gRPC and WebSocket need protocol-aware replacements
📈 Scale Stateless request/response scales by adding instances; connection-based options scale by nodes × connections; queues scale by consumers until a shared downstream becomes the limit
🔧 Ops complexity The real decision axis. Lightest to heaviest: REST < SSE < GraphQL ≈ gRPC < queue < WebSocket
🐛 Debuggability curl beats every alternative tool; each step away from plain HTTP costs you reproducibility during an incident

16. Real World Usage

Large platforms converge on a per-consumer policy rather than one protocol: REST at the public edge, gRPC internally, GraphQL for the first-party app tier, events for cross-domain propagation. The interesting part is that this is nearly always described as an explicit policy, not an accident.

LLM product APIs are the current clearest example of the framework's output: HTTP+SSE for interactive completions, 202 plus polling for batch, WebSocket only where audio flows upward — three different answers within one product, each derived from the traffic shape.

Public postmortems on API migrations consistently show the cost sitting where this framework predicts: not in the protocol, but in reimplementing auth, rate limiting, tracing and retries for the new one.

17. Acronym Decoder

RPC — Remote Procedure Call: the model where a network call looks like a function call, which is why a schema and stubs come with it. DLQ — Dead-Letter Queue: where a message goes after n failed attempts, so a poison message stops blocking its partition. SSE — Server-Sent Events: the name is the constraint, one direction only.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 97-sync-vs-async.md — question one, and the biggest fork in the framework

  • 89-rest.md, 92-grpc.md, 94-graphql.md — the three request/response options

  • 74-choosing-realtime-transport.md — the streaming column of this table, in depth

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 101-schema-contracts-compatibility.md — the contract layer under whichever option you chose

  • 102-api-authentication.md — the cross-cutting concern that diverges first when you have several protocols

  • 103-api-versioning-deprecation.md — how the chosen contract changes over years

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Webhooks — the answer when the consumer is a backend you don't operate

  • A shared database — sometimes proposed, almost always wrong across service boundaries; the coupling is worse than any protocol here

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • An API gateway — where public REST is translated to internal gRPC, and where auth and rate limiting live once

  • A schema registry — one home for .proto, OpenAPI and event schemas, with compatibility gates in CI

  • Cross-folder: gateway and mesh placement → Section 11; streaming transports → Section 8; MCP and agent transports → 99-ai-stack-protocols.md

19. System Design Application

Skipped — this is a selection framework rather than a system. Its architect-level treatment is discharged by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up (setting a per-consumer API policy across a platform), and the system-level designs live in 97-sync-vs-async.md §19 and 98-long-running-jobs.md §19.

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
What counts as a breaking change, precisely?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Generate the spec from the code, or the code from the spec?
Why both directions of compatibility are required
Contract testing, briefly
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Describing an HTTP contract — OpenAPI Specification

  • What is and isn't a safe schema change — protobuf.dev: Proto Best Practices

  • Introspection as a living contract — graphql.org: Best practices

  • Signalling a contract's end of life — RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Backward vs forward compatible? Backward: new server, old client works. Forward: old server, new client's data doesn't break it.
Why is a hand-maintained OpenAPI file dangerous? It drifts. A spec that disagrees with the implementation is worse than none — clients trust it.
The one automated control that matters? A breaking-change check in CI, so a violation fails a PR rather than a deploy.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A contract is only real if something enforces it. Protobuf enforces at compile time via generated code, GraphQL via an introspectable schema that can't drift from the implementation, and OpenAPI via nothing at all unless you generate it from the code or validate requests against it at runtime. The rules are the same everywhere: additive changes are safe, removals and type changes are not, and the dangerous case is silent misinterpretation rather than a parse error. The control that actually works is a breaking-change detector in CI, comparing this commit's schema to the last released one.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What counts as a breaking change, precisely?

Removing anything a client might depend on — a field, an endpoint, an enum value, a method. Tightening anything: making an optional field required, narrowing a type, adding a validation rule that previously-valid requests now fail. Changing meaning while keeping the shape — repurposing status values, changing a unit from cents to rupees — which is the worst class because nothing errors anywhere. And in protobuf specifically, changing a field's number or reusing a deleted one, which produces silently misread data because the wire format carries numbers, not names.

What's safe: adding an optional field, adding an endpoint or method, adding an enum value if clients handle unknown values (which is why protobuf enums need a zero UNSPECIFIED and why clients should treat unrecognised values as "unknown" rather than crashing), and relaxing validation.

The distinction that makes this operationally useful is that both directions matter. Backward compatibility — a new server serving old clients — is the one everyone thinks about. Forward compatibility — an old server receiving data from a newer client — matters whenever you can't control deploy order, which in practice is always: during a rolling deploy both versions run simultaneously.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Generate the spec from the code, or the code from the spec?

Code-first generates OpenAPI from annotations or types in the implementation. The spec can never drift, because it's derived, and the developer workflow is unchanged. The cost is that the contract becomes an output rather than a decision — you discover what you've published after writing it, design review happens against generated artefacts, and it's easy to leak internal shapes into a public API because they were convenient in the handler.

Spec-first writes the contract as the design artefact and generates server stubs and client SDKs from it. The contract gets reviewed before implementation, which is exactly what you want for a public or cross-team API, and every consumer gets a generated client. It costs a heavier workflow and a generation pipeline people will route around under deadline pressure.

My split is by audience. Spec-first for anything external or cross-team, because the review is the point and the contract outlives the implementation. Code-first for internal APIs with one consumer, where drift is the bigger risk than under-review. What is not acceptable either way is a hand-maintained spec that neither generates nor is generated — it drifts within weeks, and a wrong contract is more dangerous than a missing one because clients act on it.

4. Quick Comparison Table

OpenAPI Protobuf GraphQL schema
Enforcement none by default; runtime validation or codegen compile-time via generated code runtime, introspectable
Can drift from implementation yes — the central risk no no
Compatibility rules conventional, you define them explicit and well-documented explicit; deprecation is first-class
Automated breaking-change check via diff tooling mature tooling, standard practice via schema diff
Consumer discovery published document shared repo / registry introspection query
When you'd actually pick it HTTP APIs, public and partner gRPC and event payloads GraphQL APIs

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Why both directions of compatibility are required

During a rolling deploy, version n and version n+1 run at the same time, and both directions of every call happen: a new client may hit an old server, and an old client may hit a new one. So a change is only safe if it is both backward and forward compatible for the duration of the rollout — which is the formal reason "add the field, deploy, then start writing it, deploy, then start reading it" is three releases rather than one. Skipping the intermediate step is the most common self-inflicted compatibility incident, and it looks like a partial outage that resolves itself as the rollout completes, which makes it easy to misdiagnose.

Contract testing, briefly

Schema compatibility says the shape still parses; it says nothing about whether the consumer's expectations still hold. Consumer-driven contract testing closes that gap: each consumer publishes the interactions it depends on, and the provider's CI verifies it still satisfies all of them. It catches semantic breaks — a field that's now always empty, a status value that stopped being emitted — which no schema diff can see. The cost is a shared contract repository and consumer discipline, so it earns its place when several teams depend on one provider and integration environments are too slow to be the safety net.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't hand-maintain a spec. It drifts, and clients trust it. Generate it, or validate against it at runtime; ideally both.

  • Don't treat "it still parses" as compatible. Semantic changes — a repurposed enum value, a changed unit, a field that's now always null — pass every schema check and break every consumer. Those need contract tests or a version bump.

  • Don't rely on review to catch breaking changes. Reviewers miss them consistently, because the dangerous ones look trivial. Automate the diff.

  • Don't version an internal schema per consumer. A compatibility matrix across teams is unmanageable; additive evolution plus a deprecation window is what scales.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Adding a required field is backward compatible because old clients just won't send it."

✅ Reality: That's the definition of breaking — every existing client's request now fails validation. Add it as optional with a default, migrate clients, then tighten in a later release if you must. The three-step dance is the cost of not breaking people.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought backward compatibility was the whole story. Forward compatibility is equally load-bearing, because during any rolling deploy the old version is receiving data written by the new one. Designing for one direction produces a system that's broken for exactly the length of every deploy — long enough to page someone, short enough to be dismissed as a blip.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 90-rest-api-design.md — the contract decisions a spec has to describe

  • 92-grpc.md — protobuf's field-number rules, the strictest version of these ideas

  • 103-api-versioning-deprecation.md — what to do when a breaking change is genuinely necessary

  • 93-grpc-in-production.md — the CI gate in the context of a multi-team gRPC estate

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
What must you actually check when validating a JWT?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Bearer tokens or mTLS for service-to-service calls?
Why token lifetime is the central knob
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • OAuth 2.0 security guidance, current — RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

  • JWT pitfalls, normatively — RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

  • Certificate-bound tokens and mTLS client auth — RFC 8705: OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication

  • Signing requests without a bearer token — RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The JWT validation step people skip? Pinning the expected algorithm. Trusting the token's own alg header is the classic break.
Why can't you revoke a stateless JWT? Nothing is consulted at validation time. You need short expiry plus a refresh, or a denylist.
What does a bearer token fundamentally mean? Whoever holds it is you. No proof of possession — hence TLS, short lifetimes, and narrow scope.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Five mechanisms, each answering a different question. API keys identify a caller and nothing more — simple, long-lived, and only as safe as the places they get pasted. OAuth2 is delegation: a user authorises a third party to act on their behalf, with scopes. JWTs are a token format that lets you validate without a lookup, which is why they're fast and why revocation is hard. mTLS authenticates the client at the transport, which is the idiomatic answer inside a service mesh. HMAC signing proves a request came from you and wasn't altered, which is what webhooks need because there's no session.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What must you actually check when validating a JWT?

Six things, and each has a real failure attached. Verify the signature against a key you trust, obtained from your own configuration or a JWKS endpoint you control — never from a URL inside the token. Pin the expected algorithm rather than trusting the token's alg header, because accepting none, or accepting HS256 where you expected RS256 and thereby letting the public key be used as an HMAC secret, is the canonical JWT break. Check exp, and nbf if present, with a small clock-skew allowance. Check iss and aud, or a token minted for a different service will validate perfectly against yours. And check whatever scopes or claims authorise the specific operation, because a valid token is authentication, not authorisation.

The property behind all of this is that a JWT is validated locally — no network call, no shared state. That's the entire performance argument, and it's also why revocation is hard: nothing is consulted, so a stolen token is valid until it expires. Which is why short lifetimes, a refresh token held somewhere safer, and a denylist for the emergency case are the standard mitigations rather than optional hardening.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Bearer tokens or mTLS for service-to-service calls?

Bearer tokens are flexible and easy to reason about: mint a short-lived token per service identity, carry it in a header, validate it locally, scope it to what the caller may do. Rotation is a token refresh, not a deploy, and the same mechanism works from a browser, a partner, or a service. The weakness is inherent to the word "bearer" — anyone holding the token is you. It leaks through logs, error reports, proxy traces and screenshots, and there's no proof the presenter is its rightful owner.

mTLS moves authentication to the transport: both sides present certificates, identity is bound to the key, and there is no credential in the request to leak. Inside a service mesh it's close to free, because the sidecars do issuance, rotation and validation. Its costs are a certificate lifecycle you must actually operate — short-lived certs, automated rotation, a CA whose compromise is total — and that it authenticates the workload, not the end user, so you still need a token or a propagated identity for user-level authorisation.

The mature pattern is both, layered: mTLS between services for transport identity, plus a token carrying the end-user's identity and scopes through the call chain. RFC 8705's certificate-bound tokens formalise the combination by tying a token to the TLS client certificate, so a stolen token is useless without the corresponding key — which removes the bearer weakness precisely where it hurts most.

4. Quick Comparison Table

API key OAuth2 + JWT mTLS HMAC signature
Answers which caller is this? did the user authorise this app? which workload is this? did this request really come from you, unaltered?
Revocation delete the key hard (short expiry + denylist) revoke/expire the cert rotate the secret
Leak impact full access until rotated until expiry none — key never travels until rotated
Where it's carried header Authorization: Bearer TLS handshake signature header over the raw body
Best fit simple server-to-server, low-risk user delegation, public APIs service mesh, internal calls webhooks, callbacks
Main pitfall pasted into repos and logs alg confusion, missing aud, long expiry CA and rotation operations verifying re-serialised bodies, no timestamp

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Why token lifetime is the central knob

A stateless token cannot be revoked, so its lifetime is your exposure window: a leaked token is valid for exactly that long. Short access tokens (minutes) plus a longer-lived refresh token held in a safer store gives you revocation with a bounded delay — you revoke the refresh token, and the access token dies at its next expiry. The cost is a refresh round trip and an auth server that must be highly available, because every client depends on it.

The arithmetic worth stating: with a 15-minute access token, the worst-case window between revoking access and it taking effect is 15 minutes. If your threat model can't tolerate that, you need introspection on every request — which means a lookup, which means you gave up the stateless property you chose JWTs for. Naming that trade honestly is better than pretending short expiry is the same as revocation.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't put tokens or keys in URLs. Query strings land in access logs, proxy logs, browser history and Referer headers. Authorization headers do not. This is why EventSource's inability to set headers is a real design problem rather than an inconvenience.

  • Don't use long-lived API keys for anything high-value without a rotation story. They end up in repositories, CI configs and support tickets, and "we'd rotate it" is not a control unless rotation is automated and tested.

  • Don't validate JWTs in every service independently. Divergent validation is how one service ends up accepting tokens the others reject. Validate at the gateway, propagate identity inward, and make the mesh enforce transport identity.

  • Don't rely on mTLS alone for user-facing authorisation. It tells you which workload is calling, not which user is behind the request. You need both, and conflating them is a real authorisation gap.

  • Don't hand-roll request signing when RFC 9421 exists. Bespoke schemes reliably forget the timestamp, sign a re-serialised body, or compare digests non-constant-time.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "JWTs are more secure than session cookies."

✅ Reality: They're differently shaped, not more secure. A session id is trivially revocable because it's looked up; a JWT trades that away for stateless validation. If you're storing a JWT in a cookie and hitting a database on every request anyway, you have a session with extra parsing.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated exp as the security boundary and stopped there. aud matters just as much — without checking it, a perfectly valid token minted for a different service in the same estate validates against yours, and every signature check passes. It's a one-line check that closes a whole class of cross-service confusion.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • TLS and certificate handling → Section 5 — the substrate mTLS extends

  • 95-webhooks.md — where HMAC signing is the only workable mechanism

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 100-api-choice-framework.md — auth is the cross-cutting concern that diverges first across protocols

  • Cross-folder: gateway placement and where validation happens → Section 11; agent egress and tool authorisation → Agentic folder

How do you actually retire a version without breaking people?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
How long do you support the old version?
The headers, concretely
The arithmetic of a long tail
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Machine-readable deprecation signalling — RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field

  • The removal date, as a header — RFC 8594: The Sunset HTTP Header Field

  • Linking to the migration guide from the response — RFC 8288: Web Linking

  • Content negotiation, if you version by media type — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two headers that make deprecation machine-readable? Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594), plus a Link rel="deprecation" to the guide.
The cheapest versioning strategy? Not needing one — additive-only change, so v1 never has to become v2.
What must you have before you can retire a version? Per-consumer usage telemetry. You cannot turn off what you can't attribute.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The best versioning strategy is not shipping a new version. Additive-only change — new optional fields, new endpoints, new enum values that clients tolerate — keeps one contract alive for years, and most "we need v2" moments are a design decision that could have been additive. When a genuine break is unavoidable, run both versions in parallel, signal the old one with Deprecation and Sunset headers plus a link to the migration guide, and drive retirement off per-consumer usage telemetry rather than a calendar. Without that telemetry you can announce a sunset but you cannot safely execute one.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

How do you actually retire a version without breaking people?

Five steps, and the order matters. First, publish the new version and the migration guide together — a deprecation notice with nowhere to migrate to is just a threat. Second, mark every response from the old version with Deprecation (when it became deprecated) and Sunset (when it stops working), plus Link rel="deprecation" pointing at the guide, so the signal reaches machines and not only a changelog nobody reads. Third, instrument per-consumer usage on the old version — which client, which endpoints, how often — because the retirement decision is made on that data. Fourth, contact the remaining consumers directly, repeatedly, and by name. Fifth, brown-out before you black-out: return errors for a scheduled window — an hour, then a day — so the remaining callers discover the dependency while someone is watching, rather than at 3am on cut-off day.

The step that gets skipped is the third one, and it's the one that makes the rest possible. Without per-consumer attribution you're looking at an aggregate request count that never quite reaches zero, and nobody can tell whether the remaining traffic is a health check or a bank.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How long do you support the old version?

The honest answer is that it depends on who your consumers are and what it costs you to keep both alive. Internal consumers you can see and page are weeks. First-party mobile apps are as long as old app versions stay installed — often six to twelve months, because you cannot force an upgrade. Public partners are typically six to twenty-four months, and enterprise contracts sometimes fix it in writing. The mistake is picking a number without asking which of these you have.

The cost side is what usually gets under-weighted. Two versions means two code paths, two sets of tests, every bug fixed twice, and — worse — a data model that must satisfy both, which quietly constrains the design you were trying to move to. That drag is why long support windows aren't free generosity: they slow the thing the new version was for.

So I'd set the window by consumer class, publish it as policy before the first deprecation, and spend the effort on making it unnecessary. Additive evolution, tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields, and enums with an explicit unknown value remove most reasons to break, and each break you avoid is a support window you never pay for.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Strategy Visible to caches/logs Client effort Cost to you When you'd actually pick it
URL path (/v1/) ✅ everywhere trivial routing per version Public and partner APIs — the practical default
Media type (Accept: …v2+json) ❌ needs Vary discipline easy to get wrong cache-key configuration Genuine representation variants, not breaking changes
Custom header (X-API-Version) ❌ easy validation everywhere Internal APIs where you control every client
No versioning, additive only n/a none design discipline Everything you can manage this way — the cheapest option by far

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The headers, concretely

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

The arithmetic of a long tail

Version migrations follow a long tail: a large fraction of traffic moves in the first weeks, and the last few percent takes as long as everything before it. So the useful metric is not "percentage of traffic on v1" — which flatters you — but the count of distinct consumers still calling v1, because retiring is gated on the last one, not on the volume. A version at 0.3% of traffic and 40 distinct consumers is much further from retirement than one at 4% with a single well-known caller. Track and report the count.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't version endpoint-by-endpoint. /v1/orders alongside /v3/customers creates a compatibility matrix nobody can reason about. Version the API surface.

  • Don't announce a sunset without per-consumer telemetry. You'll reach the date unable to tell whether the remaining traffic is a monitoring probe or someone's payroll run, and you'll extend indefinitely.

  • Don't ship v2 as a rewrite. The larger the delta, the fewer consumers migrate, and the longer you run both. A small, well-documented break gets adopted; a redesign gets ignored.

  • Don't rely on a changelog as the notification channel. Response headers, SDK warnings and direct email to identified consumers are what actually land.

  • Don't hard cut without a brown-out. A scheduled error window while your team is watching converts a future incident into a controlled discovery.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Adding a field is always backward compatible."

✅ Reality: It's compatible only if clients tolerate unknown fields — a strict schema validator, a language binding that errors on extra keys, or a client asserting an exact response shape will break. "Be tolerant in what you accept" is a property you have to state as a documented client requirement, not one you can assume.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I thought the versioning mechanism was the hard part and argued about URL versus header. The mechanism is a twenty-minute decision; the hard parts are the discipline that avoids needing it and the per-consumer telemetry that lets you finish a retirement. Choosing the elegant mechanism and skipping those two is how an API ends up with four live versions and none of them retirable.
